I wonder what "problem" his extra base pair was actually solving ...

Do we really need greater information density? There's already tons of space within the genome we don't use.
Sure, what is the worst that could happen?

This article is making a big fuss about nothing, really. The way human cells, or any living thing on Earth using DNA, synthesize proteins is by effectively translating segments of 3 bases (A, T, C and G) into specific protein "lego pieces", the amino acids, that, depending on the following segments, result in a different protein when put together. With segments of 3 built from 4 different bases, we get a maximum of 64 amino acids (4^3 = 64). There's no reason to add another 2 bases (P and Z, as mentioned in the article) to achieve more possible combinations for amino acids when we're only using 20 of 61 possible (3 are used to either start, stop or signal the end of the protein when building it from the mRNA).

This part was the most... let's say interesting:

Benner has lofty goals for his synthetic molecules. He wants to create an alternative genetic system in which proteins—intricately folded molecules that perform essential biological functions—are unnecessary. I can't quite imagine why he would think that. Proteins are most essential to life, they act as the messenger between cells (and different parts of the same cell), catalysts for chemical reactions (Why do you think does almost every human on earth have an average body temperature of 37 degree celsius? Those reactions would normally only take place at much higher temperatures, effectively killing you. Catalysts make sure those reactions happen at a feasible temperature) and are used to build the vast majority of tissue: muscles, hair, eyes... All made from proteins. Life without them, or an equivalent repertoire of molecules, just isn't possible.

What the article doesn't say is whether or not they checked their modified DNA for blockages of the new parts. Are they just marked as "spam" and ignored, or have they actually served a purpose? Yes, it's nice that he managed to squeeze in more stuff without disrupting the structure of the DNA, but it really doesn't serve much of a purpose.

Wages are simply the price of labour, and the freer the market the faster economic growth will be. So assuming that in the long run you would consider a faster rate of economic growth to be better, the freer the labour market the better. A free labour market will price wages at fair value, (or as low as workers are willing to accept given competition for labour), minimizing unemployment and forcing up wages for workers who have skills which are in high demand and low supply.
